findings.reason: Proof step 3.2 applies the zero-integral criterion to g(r) and asserts ∫g(r)=D without establishing measurability, integrability, or the integral identity. From step 2.1, φ(r), r∈L¹; Q is a probability measure, so 1∈L¹. Use the published L¹ linearity result and the available measurability result to establish g(r)∈L¹ and ∫g(r)=D before applying [F12].

Proof steps 1.2–1.3 apply Tonelli/Fubini to fixed-θ slices, but joint measurability on Θ×X×Z alone is not shown to make those slices product-measurable. Supply the section argument (reduce complex h to its real and imaginary parts) and define hp on the possible p=∞ null set before treating it as a complex L¹ function.
The Definition accepts a caller stopping rule but never tests it. Specify when the rule is checked and what the procedure returns when it fires, as required by the approved design.

The approved design requires Newton-decrement stopping. The Definition provides only unspecified stopping rules and a generic post-update callback. State the decrement criterion, threshold and check point, and specify the output/status when a positive-definite solve is unavailable.

The statement gives the bound for every k≥1, although gradient descent may stop at zero gradient or at the caller's rule; for μ=L it can stop after one update. State the bound for every generated iterate or explicitly define the continued fixed-step recursion.

With the approved decrement stopping rule, a nonstationary iterate may terminate before a line search. Qualify full-step acceptance and the rate for updates the algorithm attempts, or state the result for the continued Newton iteration.

The all-k formula uses a continued fixed-step sequence, while the algorithm can stop at zero gradient or at the caller's rule. Make explicit whether the example concerns the continued update sequence or only generated iterates.
